arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Tripp argued that a criminal alien does not escape mandatory detention just because the government delayed their arrest.
Ms. Wang argued that the government's reading contradicts the statute's text, structure, and purpose in at least three ways.
Ms. Wang stated that the government's view negates Congress's directive to use finite detention resources on those released from criminal custody.
Mr. Tripp noted that aliens are often released before the Department of Homeland Security is even aware of the release.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case tests the interaction between two federal statutes. One mandates detention for certain criminal aliens. The other allows the government to set its own arrest timelines. The core conflict is whether a delay in arrest voids the mandatory detention requirement.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: The government wants the Court to confirm that mandatory detention applies regardless of how long the arrest delay lasts.
The alien wants the Court to rule that a significant delay in arrest ends the mandatory detention requirement.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: The government argues that the statutory text mandates detention for criminal aliens, and a delay in arrest does not change this legal obligation.
The alien argues that the statute directs detention resources to those released from criminal custody, so a long delay negates the mandate.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case determines whether criminal aliens face indefinite detention without bond hearings. It defines the government's power to delay arrests. It impacts the balance between public safety and individual liberty. It clarifies the scope of mandatory detention laws.
